title: Classical curvature
one_line_summary: Builds curvature from the ground up with classical calculus in flat 3-space: the osculating circle and Frenet-Serret frame for curves, principal curvatures and the second fundamental form for surfaces, Gauss's intrinsic curvature as det(g^-1 K), and a sketch of how Riemann generalized it to n dimensions.
role_in_book: Opens Part V, the book's second, more rigorous pass through geometry. Having already used the Riemann tensor physically (ch11) and applied it to cosmology and black holes, the authors step back to the pre-tensor, embedding-based picture of curvature so that the coordinate-free machinery of chs 31-36 has a concrete ancestor. It is flagged as optional, but it is where intrinsic versus extrinsic curvature is made computable, and its exercises preview the 3+1 hypersurface language (projection operator, extrinsic curvature tensor, Gauss-Codazzi equations).

assumed_background.topic: Differentiation, Taylor expansion to second order, limits
Dot and cross products, triple product, orthonormal triads in R^3
Eigenvalues, eigenvectors, determinant and trace of 2x2 matrices; diagonalizing a symmetric matrix by rotation
Metric components, line element ds^2 = g_ij dx^i dx^j, inverse metric and index raising
Basis vectors as partial derivatives of position, e_mu = dX/dx^mu
Connection coefficients from the metric (Christoffel symbols)
Riemann tensor in terms of metric derivatives, eqn 11.22
Parallel transport around a loop (for Exercise 30.2)
Covariant derivative and unit timelike normals, signature (-,+,+,+) (for Exercises 30.7-30.8)
Uniform circular motion: centripetal force v^2/r (Exercise 30.1)

learning_objectives: Reader can define the curvature of a plane curve as the reciprocal radius of the osculating circle and compute it three ways: tangent turning rate d(theta)/ds, second derivative of height above the tangent line, and |dt/ds|.
Reader can construct the Frenet-Serret frame (t, p, b) for a space curve, define curvature and torsion, and write and interpret the antisymmetric Frenet-Serret matrix equation.
Reader can expand a surface's height above its tangent plane as a quadratic form, diagonalize it by rotating axes, and read off the principal curvatures and principal directions.
Reader can explain why Gauss wanted a curvature measurable from inside the surface and state the theorema egregium.
Reader can compute Gaussian curvature from the Gauss-map area ratio dOmega/dA using a surface parametrization X(x^1, x^2).

Reader can decompose the derivative of a basis vector into a tangential part (connection coefficients) and a normal part K_mu nu (Gauss's formula), and compute K_mu nu for a cylinder, paraboloid and sphere.
Reader can derive that the normal curvature of a curve through a point is kappa_n = K_mu nu t^mu t^nu and, via a Lagrange multiplier, that its extremes are the eigenvalues of g^{-1}K.
Reader can distinguish intrinsic curvature K = det K / det g = k1 k2 from the trace k1 + k2, and explain with the cylinder and sphere why only the former is visible to surface dwellers.
Reader can state Riemann's counting argument in outline and relate Gaussian curvature to the Riemann tensor via K = R_1212 / g in two dimensions.
Reader can, through the exercises, meet Weingarten's equation, projection onto a spacelike hypersurface, the induced metric and derivative, and the Gauss-Codazzi equations.

teaching_approach.summary: A historically ordered, dimension-climbing build-up. Each new dimension repeats the same three representations: a geometric comparison shape (circle, then ellipse/quadric), a coordinate Taylor expansion of height above a tangent line or plane, and a vector/basis-derivative formalism in flat embedding space. The payoff is reached by pushing the embedding formalism until the embedding drops out (det g^-1 K is intrinsic), then handing off to Riemann in words rather than proofs. Heavy use of boxed Examples keeps the main text short; margin notes carry etymology, history and caveats. The chapter explicitly labels itself skippable and classical, in contrast to the coordinate-free Part V to follow.
narrative_arc: Motivating question: what number should measure how bent a path is? Guitar outline and steering-wheel intuition.
Model: compare the curve with a circle; osculating circle from two nearby normals, kappa = 1/rho.
Alternative representations: angle swept by unit tangents per arc length; height above the tangent line as a parabola, kappa = y''.
Formalism for curves in 3-space: position vector X(s), unit tangent, principal normal, binormal, torsion, Frenet-Serret matrix.
Upgrade to surfaces: height above the tangent plane as a symmetric quadratic form; rotate to principal axes (Euler's perpendicularity); sphere check.
Problem: all of this uses a surrounding space. Gauss's goal of an insider's curvature; theorema egregium shown via the formidable metric formula; sphere and plane checks.
Vector formalism for surfaces: Gauss-map area ratio dOmega/dA and its cross-product formula.
Split basis-vector derivatives into in-surface (Gamma) and normal (K_mu nu) parts; compute K_mu nu for a cylinder.
Link K_mu nu to curvature: normal curvature of curves through a point, extremize with constraint, eigenvalues of g^{-1}K.
Interpretation: determinant is intrinsic (Gaussian) curvature, trace is extrinsic; cylinder versus sphere; paraboloid and sphere examples.
Generalization: Riemann's degrees-of-freedom argument, sectional curvature Q(W), the 1861 Paris paper, K = R_1212/g; hand-off to the modern treatment.
Exercises extend to Weingarten's equation and to the 3+1 projection formalism with Gauss and Codazzi equations.
signature_moves: Same curvature measured three ways for a curve (circle radius, turning angle per length, second derivative of height) so learners see one invariant through several lenses.
Dimensional analogy of ratios: angle swept on the unit circle per arc length for curves becomes solid angle swept on the unit sphere per area for surfaces.
Car steering-wheel intuition for curvature before any formula.
Physical props for intrinsic vs extrinsic: a tin can wrapped by a flat grid sheet, paper that cannot cover a sphere without cutting, and shoelaces that can always be straightened.
Splitting a derivative of a basis vector into tangential and normal components, a template reused later for connections and extrinsic curvature.
Deriving principal curvatures as a constrained eigenvalue problem, then extracting determinant and trace as the two invariants.
Showing Gauss's full formula in all its ugliness to dramatize why better methods (Riemann tensor, Cartan) are wanted, without asking the reader to use it.
Etymology and literary asides (osculate = kiss, egregious) used to make terminology memorable.

sections.title: Part V opener: Geometry
sections.summary: A one-page road map for Part V: classical curvature (ch30), modern tensors (31-32), coordinate-free derivatives (33-34), curvature revisited (35), Cartan's method (36), volume forms (37), integrals and Stokes (38), plus Appendix C. It reassures physics readers that Einstein himself needed Marcel Grossmann's help with differential geometry.
key_moves: Positions the geometry part as a rigorous second pass whose tools are used in Part VI.
Normalizes unfamiliarity with the mathematics by the Einstein-Grossmann anecdote.

sections.title: Chapter opening
sections.summary: Frames the chapter as the classical, calculus-based history of curvature, explicitly optional for readers who want only the modern coordinate-free approach. It names the arc: Euler and Cauchy for curves culminating in the Frenet-Serret equations; Gauss for surfaces measured from within; Riemann for higher dimensions and GR.
key_moves: Marks the chapter as skippable and classical.
Previews the historical chain Euler/Cauchy to Frenet-Serret to Gauss to Riemann.

sections.title: Curvature of a line
sections.summary: Curvature of a planar path is motivated by how fast tangents turn (steering wheel on a guitar-shaped road). The circle is chosen as the comparison shape: two nearby normals meet at the centre of curvature, giving the osculating circle with radius rho and curvature kappa = 1/rho. Example 30.1 re-expresses this as the angle swept by unit tangents on a unit circle divided by arc length, kappa = d(theta)/ds. A coordinate version measures height y above the tangent line so that kappa = d^2y/dx^2, justified in Example 30.2 by Taylor expansion and by matching to a circle's height x^2/(2 rho).
key_moves: Pick a reference figure (circle) whose curvature is obviously uniform and scaled by 1/radius.
Locate the centre of curvature as the limit intersection of two nearby normals.
Map unit tangents onto a unit circle so curvature becomes swept angle per arc length.
Use a tangent-aligned coordinate so the linear Taylor term vanishes; the quadratic coefficient is the curvature.
Match to a circle's small-angle height rho(1 - cos theta) ~ x^2/(2 rho); margin note stresses that locally the comparison is really to a parabola.

sections.title: Curvature with vectors
sections.summary: Works in flat 3-space with a curve X(s). The unit tangent t = dX/ds is expanded on basis vectors e_mu = dX/dx^mu. Differentiating t.t = 1 shows dt/ds is perpendicular to t, defining the principal normal p and curvature kappa; Example 30.3 checks kappa equals d(theta)/ds via an isosceles-triangle chord. The binormal b = t x p completes an orthonormal triad; Example 30.4 shows db/ds lies along p, defining torsion tau. Differentiating p = b x t yields dp/ds = tau b - kappa t, and the three results assemble into the antisymmetric Frenet-Serret matrix system: two scalar functions kappa and tau describe a space curve.
key_moves: Normalization t.t = 1 differentiated gives orthogonality of t and dt/ds.
Chord between unit tangents has length 2 sin(dtheta/2) ~ dtheta, proving |dt/ds| = dtheta/ds.
Unit length of b and orthogonality b.t = 0, differentiated, force db/ds to be along p.
Cyclic cross-product relations of the triad let dp/ds be computed from the other two.
Package as a 3x3 antisymmetric matrix acting on the triad.

sections.title: Two-dimensional surfaces
sections.summary: For surfaces in flat 3-space a single sphere will not do, since bending generally differs by direction. Euler's result that the directions of maximal and minimal bending are perpendicular lets curvature be encoded in a symmetric 2x2 tensor K_ij: the height above the tangent plane is z = (1/2) K_ij x^i x^j. Example 30.5 rotates axes to diagonalize, giving principal curvatures kappa_1, kappa_2 and checks a sphere (both 1/a). The authors then note this depends on an embedding and introduce Gauss's programme of intrinsic measurement: Gaussian curvature K and the theorema egregium. Example 30.6 displays Gauss's explicit formula for K in terms of g_ij and its first and second derivatives, checking K = 1/a^2 for a sphere and 0 for the plane.
key_moves: Generalize the curve's parabola to a quadric height function with a symmetric coefficient matrix.
Diagonalize by a rotation of the tangent-plane axes (principal axes).
Check with a sphere resting on a plane.
Pose the insider problem: inhabitants cannot step outside to see the embedding.
Present Gauss's metric-only formula (with locally flat coordinates as the starting assumption) and check it on sphere and plane.

sections.title: Gauss' equation
sections.summary: By analogy with swept angle per length, Gaussian curvature is defined as the area swept by unit normals on the unit sphere per area on the surface, dOmega/dA. With a parametrization X(x^1, x^2), basis vectors e_1, e_2 and unit normal n = e_1 x e_2 / |e_1 x e_2|, Example 30.7 derives K = n.(dn/dx^1 x dn/dx^2)/|e_1 x e_2|. The more modern route decomposes the derivative of a basis vector into tangential connection terms Gamma^lambda_mu nu e_lambda and a normal part K_mu nu n; projecting on n gives Gauss's equation K_mu nu = (de_nu/dx^mu).n. Example 30.8 computes it for a cylinder: only K_theta theta = -a is non-zero.
key_moves: Promote the 1D ratio (angle/length) to 2D (solid angle/area).
Area elements from cross products of coordinate derivatives; triple product with n fixes the sign.
Normalization factor of n treated as constant when differentiating (margin note 15).
Decompose de_nu/dx^mu into in-surface and normal pieces; the normal coefficient is K_mu nu.
Cylinder: straight rulings give zero, circular direction gives -a.

sections.title: Intrinsic and extrinsic curvature
sections.summary: For a curve in the surface through P, dt/ds splits into an in-surface part kappa_g e and a normal part kappa_n n. Writing d/ds = t^nu d/dx^nu and using Gauss's equation gives kappa_n = K_mu nu t^mu t^nu (margin note introduces first and second fundamental forms). Following Gauss, all curves through P are considered: Example 30.9 extremizes kappa_n under g_mu nu t^mu t^nu = 1 with a Lagrange multiplier, giving the eigenvalue problem for A = g^{-1}K whose eigenvalues are the extremal normal curvatures. Two invariants follow: det A = det K/det g = k1 k2 is the Gaussian (intrinsic) curvature, and Tr A = k1 + k2 is called the extrinsic curvature. A cylinder (tin can, Fig. 30.8) has k1 = -1/a, k2 = 0 so zero intrinsic curvature; a sphere cannot be flattened. Example 30.10 computes both invariants for a paraboloid at its vertex (uv and u+v) and a sphere (1/a^2 and -2/a). A note explains that curves have no intrinsic curvature.
key_moves: Project the acceleration of a unit-speed curve onto the surface normal.
Chain rule converts d/ds into t^nu partial derivatives, giving a quadratic form in t.
Constrained extremum with the metric as constraint produces the mixed tensor g^{lambda mu} K_mu nu.
Contract the eigen-equation with t to show eigenvalues equal extremal normal curvatures.
Identify determinant (intrinsic) and trace (extrinsic) as the basis-independent invariants.
Cylinder vs sphere as the decisive contrast; shoelaces for 1D.

sections.title: Riemann's project
sections.summary: Riemann sought an intrinsic curvature for n-dimensional spaces. His counting: a symmetric metric has n(n+1)/2 component functions, coordinate changes use n, so n(n-1)/2 functions carry genuine geometric content. He introduced a quadratic quantity Q(W) on each two-plane W, with -3Q giving the Gaussian curvature of that section, and claimed knowledge of Q on the n(n-1)/2 independent planes fixes the metric. In an 1861 Paris prize essay on heat conduction he wrote down what is now the Riemann tensor and stated flatness as its vanishing; Q(W) is proportional to R(X,Y,X,Y). The chapter gives the two-dimensional link K = R_1212/g and, in Example 30.11, outlines verifying it by combining eqn 11.22, the Christoffel formula and the 2x2 inverse metric with Gauss's formula, leaving the algebra to the reader.
concepts: degrees of freedom of a metric
key_moves: Count metric functions minus coordinate freedom to estimate genuine geometric data.
Reduce higher-dimensional curvature to Gaussian curvatures of 2D sections.
State flatness as vanishing of the Riemann tensor.
Close the loop in 2D: K equals the single independent Riemann component divided by det g.

sections.title: Chapter summary and exercises
sections.summary: Three-bullet summary (Frenet-Serret for curves, Gaussian curvature as intrinsic, Riemann's generalization) and eight exercises ranging from a mechanical definition of curvature and parallel-transport and circumference definitions of K, through matrix invariants and Weingarten's equation, to projection operators, induced metric, induced covariant derivative, extrinsic curvature tensor and the Gauss and Codazzi equations for a spacelike hypersurface.
key_moves: Exercises 30.7-30.8 re-express the chapter's embedding ideas covariantly for hypersurfaces in spacetime.

concepts.name: curvature of a curve
concepts.definition: The rate at which the unit tangent of a curve turns per unit arc length, kappa = |dt/ds| = d(theta)/ds; equivalently the reciprocal of the radius of the circle that best fits the curve at that point.
concepts.how_introduced: From a guitar outline and the steering-wheel intuition that sharper bends turn tangents faster; the circle is chosen as the yardstick and then three equivalent computations are offered.
concepts.notes: The d^2y/dx^2 form holds only in coordinates aligned with the tangent (y' = 0 at the point); the general graph formula is y''/(1+y'^2)^{3/2}, which the book does not give.

concepts.name: osculating circle
concepts.definition: The circle that touches a curve at a point P to second order: it shares the tangent and the curvature there, and its centre (centre of curvature) lies on the normal at distance rho = 1/kappa.
concepts.how_introduced: Using the fact that two normals of a circle meet at its centre, the limiting intersection of two closely spaced normals of the curve defines the centre; a margin note gives the Latin root meaning to kiss.

concepts.name: radius of curvature
concepts.definition: The distance rho from a point on a curve to its centre of curvature; the reciprocal of the curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: As the radius of the osculating circle; later principal radii rho_1, rho_2 for surfaces.

concepts.name: arc-length parametrization
concepts.definition: Parametrizing a curve by the distance s measured along it, so that dX/ds has unit length at every point.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from ch9 with a sketch of equally spaced tick marks s1, s2, ... along a curve; used to make tangents unit vectors.

concepts.name: unit tangent vector
concepts.definition: t = dX/ds, the derivative of the position on a curve with respect to arc length; it has unit length and components t^mu = dx^mu/ds on the basis e_mu = dX/dx^mu.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined for a curve X(s) embedded in flat 3-space, with a margin caution that using a position vector relies on the flat embedding and will be abandoned in curved spacetime.

concepts.name: principal normal vector
concepts.definition: The unit vector p along dt/ds; it is perpendicular to the tangent because t has constant length, and dt/ds = kappa p.
concepts.how_introduced: Differentiating t.t = 1 shows dt/ds is orthogonal to t, so its direction is named p and its magnitude kappa.
concepts.notes: Often denoted N in other texts.

concepts.name: osculating plane
concepts.definition: The plane through a point of a curve spanned by the unit tangent t and principal normal p; it is the plane in which the curve locally bends and contains the osculating circle.
concepts.how_introduced: Drawn as a hatched face of a box built on the Frenet triad; for a plane curve it never changes.

concepts.name: plane curve
concepts.definition: A curve lying entirely within one plane; its osculating plane is fixed and its torsion is zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned to contrast with general space curves before introducing the binormal and torsion.

concepts.name: binormal vector
concepts.definition: The unit vector b = t x p, normal to the osculating plane, completing a right-handed orthonormal triad with t and p.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced to span 3-space for non-planar curves; Example 30.4 then shows its derivative lies along p.

concepts.name: torsion
concepts.definition: The scalar tau defined by db/ds = -tau p; it measures how fast the osculating plane twists about the tangent, i.e. how quickly the curve leaves being planar.
concepts.how_introduced: After proving db/ds is parallel to p, its coefficient is named torsion.
concepts.notes: Not the same as the torsion of a connection met later in differential geometry; a tutor should flag the name clash. The book's sentence attributes the twisting measure to b itself; strictly it is db/ds (hence tau).

concepts.name: Frenet-Serret equations
concepts.definition: The linear system giving the arc-length derivatives of the orthonormal triad (t, p, b) of a space curve: t' = kappa p, p' = -kappa t + tau b, b' = -tau p; the coefficient matrix is antisymmetric and a curve is determined up to rigid motion by kappa(s) and tau(s).
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled from the three derivative results into a 3x3 matrix equation, presented as the milestone of classical curve theory.
formulas: \frac{d}{ds}(\mathbf t,\mathbf p,\mathbf b)^T = \begin{pmatrix}0&\kappa&0\\-\kappa&0&\tau\\0&-\tau&0\end{pmatrix}(\mathbf t,\mathbf p,\mathbf b)^T
concepts.notes: The book states that two parameters suffice but does not state the fundamental theorem of curves (existence and uniqueness up to Euclidean motion).

concepts.name: embedding
concepts.definition: Realizing a lower-dimensional space as a subset of a higher-dimensional flat space, so that its points are given by position vectors X in the larger space.
concepts.how_introduced: Used throughout for curves and surfaces in flat 3-space, then questioned: beings confined to a surface cannot use it, motivating intrinsic measures.
concepts.notes: Appendix D of GA treats embedding further.

concepts.name: principal curvatures
concepts.definition: At a point of a surface, the maximum and minimum normal curvatures over all tangent directions; they are the eigenvalues of the shape operator g^{-1}K, with reciprocal principal radii rho_1, rho_2.
concepts.how_introduced: First as the diagonal entries after rotating the height quadratic form to principal axes (30.3), then rederived as constrained extremes of kappa_n (Example 30.9).
concepts.notes: Signs depend on the choice of normal orientation; the book's examples give negative values for a sphere or cylinder with the outward normal.

concepts.name: principal directions
concepts.definition: The tangent directions in which normal curvature is extremal; when the principal curvatures differ they are perpendicular (Euler), being eigenvectors of a matrix symmetric with respect to the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Attributed to Euler as the discovery that makes two-direction curvature manageable; shown by rotating axes in Example 30.5.
concepts.notes: Euler's curvature formula kappa_n = kappa_1 cos^2 phi + kappa_2 sin^2 phi is implied but not written.

concepts.name: second fundamental form
concepts.definition: The symmetric tensor K_mu nu on a surface given by the normal component of the derivative of the basis vectors, K_mu nu = (de_nu/dx^mu).n; in tangent-plane coordinates the height of the surface is z = (1/2)K_ij x^i x^j, and F_2 = K_mu nu dx^mu dx^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: First as the coefficient matrix of the quadratic height function over the tangent plane (30.17), then as the normal part of basis-vector derivatives (Gauss's equation), with the name second fundamental form confined to a margin note.
concepts.notes: The book uses K for this tensor, for Gaussian curvature, and in Exercise 30.8 for the spacetime extrinsic curvature tensor; learners should track which is meant.

concepts.name: first fundamental form
concepts.definition: The quadratic form g_mu nu dx^mu dx^nu with g_mu nu = e_mu . e_nu, giving lengths on a surface from within; it is the line element ds^2 of the surface.
concepts.how_introduced: In a margin note that identifies the classical name with the familiar line element, noting the terminology will not be used again.
concepts.notes: Printed with dX^mu for the coordinate differentials.

concepts.name: metric tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric tensor whose components g_ij give squared distance ds^2 = g_ij dx^i dx^j between nearby points; for an embedded surface g_mu nu = e_mu . e_nu.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled in Example 30.6 as the object from which Gauss builds an intrinsic curvature; locally flat coordinates with ds^2 = (dxi^1)^2 + (dxi^2)^2 are assumed at a point.

concepts.name: surface basis vectors
concepts.definition: For a surface X(x^1, x^2) in flat 3-space, the tangent vectors e_mu = dX/dx^mu along the coordinate lines; they span the tangent plane.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by analogy with the tangent dX/ds of a curve, the surface coordinates playing the role of s.

concepts.name: unit normal
concepts.definition: The unit vector perpendicular to a surface, n = (e_1 x e_2)/|e_1 x e_2|; its orientation fixes the signs of K_mu nu and principal curvatures.
concepts.how_introduced: From the cross product of basis vectors in Example 30.7; margin note 15 explains the normalization factor is not differentiated.

concepts.name: Gauss map
concepts.definition: The map sending each point of a surface to the tip of its unit normal on the unit sphere; the ratio of image area dOmega to surface area dA at a point is the Gaussian curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: As the 2D analogue of laying unit tangents on a unit circle; the map itself is not named in the book.
formulas: K = \frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot(\partial_1\hat{\mathbf n}\times\partial_2\hat{\mathbf n})}{|\mathbf e_1\times\mathbf e_2|}
concepts.notes: Signed: a saddle's normals sweep with reversed orientation, giving negative K.

concepts.name: Gaussian curvature
concepts.definition: The scalar K = k1 k2, the product of the principal curvatures, equal to det K_mu nu / det g_mu nu, to the Gauss-map area ratio, and in 2D to R_1212/g; it depends only on the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: As Gauss's answer to the insider problem; shown first via his explicit metric formula, then via normals sweeping area, then as the determinant of g^{-1}K, and finally tied to Riemann's tensor.
concepts.notes: Exercises add parallel-transport (angle/area) and circumference-deficit definitions.

concepts.name: theorema egregium
concepts.definition: Gauss's theorem that the Gaussian curvature of a surface can be computed from the metric components and their first and second derivatives alone, so it is unchanged by bending without stretching and is measurable by surface dwellers.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by beings confined to their space; illustrated by displaying Gauss's explicit formula and checking sphere and plane; the word egregious is glossed in a margin note.
concepts.notes: The chapter never proves that det K/det g equals the metric formula; that link is asserted with 'it turns out' and partly left to exercises and Example 30.11.

concepts.name: intrinsic curvature
concepts.definition: Curvature detectable by measurements of lengths and angles made entirely within a space, independent of how it sits in any larger space; for a surface it is the Gaussian curvature.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with extrinsic bending using a tin can (unrollable) and a sphere (cannot be flattened without cutting); a margin note says curves have none.
concepts.notes: Revisits GA ch11 §11.1.

concepts.name: extrinsic curvature
concepts.definition: Curvature that describes how a space is bent within a larger embedding space; the book uses the name for the trace k1 + k2 = Tr(g^{-1}K), which is twice the mean curvature, while the full tensor K_mu nu is also called the extrinsic curvature tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: As the second invariant of the eigenvalue problem, illustrated by a cylinder that looks curved but unrolls flat.
concepts.notes: Standard terminology calls (k1+k2)/2 the mean curvature H; in GR 'extrinsic curvature' normally denotes the tensor K_ij and K its trace.

concepts.name: shape operator
aliases: mixed tensor g^{lambda mu} K_mu nu
concepts.definition: The (1,1) tensor A^lambda_nu = g^{lambda mu}K_mu nu mapping tangent vectors to tangent vectors; its eigenvalues are the principal curvatures, its determinant the Gaussian curvature, its trace k1 + k2.
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges from a Lagrange-multiplier extremization of normal curvature subject to unit length measured by the metric.
concepts.notes: Book calls it simply the matrix A; shape operator and Weingarten map are standard names.

concepts.name: normal curvature
concepts.definition: The component along the surface normal of the curvature vector dt/ds of a curve lying in the surface; it depends only on the tangent direction: kappa_n = K_mu nu t^mu t^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: By splitting dt/ds for a curve through P into tangential and normal parts and projecting onto n.

concepts.name: geodesic curvature
concepts.definition: The component of a curve's curvature vector lying in the tangent plane of the surface; it is intrinsic, and vanishes exactly for geodesics of the surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only as the unnamed coefficient kappa_g in the split of dt/ds; not developed.
concepts.notes: The name and geodesic link are our addition; a strong bridge to GA ch8-9.

concepts.name: Gauss's formula for basis-vector derivatives
concepts.definition: For an embedded surface, the derivative of a basis vector splits into a tangential part given by connection coefficients and a normal part given by the second fundamental form: de_nu/dx^mu = Gamma^lambda_mu nu e_lambda + K_mu nu n.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as the approach closest to modern differential geometry; the in-surface part previews the connection, the out-of-surface part defines K_mu nu.
concepts.notes: A margin note jokes that Gauss has too many equations for this name to be unique; Exercise 30.8 gives the different, higher-dimensional Gauss equation.

concepts.name: connection coefficients
concepts.definition: The coefficients Gamma^lambda_mu nu giving the in-space part of the change of basis vectors; for a metric-compatible torsion-free connection they are built from first derivatives of the metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Reappear as the tangential part of basis-vector derivatives on an embedded surface, and in Example 30.11 via the standard metric formula.

concepts.name: developable surface
concepts.definition: A surface with zero Gaussian curvature everywhere, which can be flattened onto a plane without stretching or tearing, such as a cylinder or cone.
concepts.how_introduced: Through the tin-can picture: a grid sheet wraps the can and lies flat; the term itself is not used.

concepts.name: Lagrange multiplier
concepts.definition: A method for extremizing a function subject to a constraint by extremizing the function minus a multiplier times the constraint.
concepts.how_introduced: Used in Example 30.9 to find extreme normal curvatures with the constraint that the tangent is unit length in the metric; the multiplier becomes the eigenvalue.

concepts.name: Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: The (0,4) tensor built from the metric and its first and second derivatives whose vanishing is the condition for flatness; filled with two vectors spanning a plane it gives the Gaussian curvature of that section.
concepts.how_introduced: Historically, as appearing in Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay; linked to Gauss's K in 2D via R_1212/g.
concepts.notes: First met in GA ch11; rigorous treatment in ch35.

concepts.name: sectional curvature
concepts.definition: The Gaussian curvature of the two-dimensional surface swept out by geodesics tangent to a two-plane W in a higher-dimensional space; it equals R(X,Y,Y,X)/(|X|^2|Y|^2 - (X.Y)^2) up to sign convention.
concepts.how_introduced: Via Riemann's quadratic function Q(W) with -3Q(W) giving the Gaussian curvature of the section W; the modern name is not used.

concepts.name: degrees of freedom of a metric
concepts.definition: The heuristic count that an n-dimensional metric has n(n+1)/2 component functions, of which n can be altered by a coordinate change, leaving n(n-1)/2 functions of genuine geometric content.
concepts.how_introduced: As Riemann's framing of when two metrics are secretly the same; a margin note derives n(n+1)/2.
concepts.notes: At a single point the Riemann tensor has n^2(n^2-1)/12 independent components (1, 6, 20 for n = 2, 3, 4), so this count is about functions, not pointwise components.

concepts.name: flatness criterion
concepts.definition: A space is flat (admits coordinates in which the metric is constant and Euclidean or Minkowskian) exactly when its Riemann tensor vanishes everywhere.
concepts.how_introduced: Credited to Riemann's 1861 paper as the answer to what makes a space flat.

concepts.name: Weingarten equation
concepts.definition: The derivative of the unit normal of a surface is tangent and given by the shape operator: dn/dx^nu = -K^mu_nu e_mu, equivalently K_mu nu = -e_mu . dn/dx^nu.
concepts.how_introduced: Only in Exercise 30.5, by differentiating t.n = 0 along a curve.

concepts.name: projection operator
concepts.definition: For a spacelike hypersurface with unit timelike normal n (n.n = -1), P^mu_nu = delta^mu_nu + n^mu n_nu removes the normal part of a vector, satisfies P^2 = P, and induces the spatial metric h = g + n n.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 30.7 only, as a first step toward describing hypersurfaces in spacetime.
concepts.notes: Sign relies on signature (-,+,+,+).

concepts.name: Gauss-Codazzi equations
concepts.definition: Relations expressing projections of the spacetime Riemann tensor onto a hypersurface in terms of the hypersurface's own Riemann tensor, its extrinsic curvature tensor K_alpha beta = -P P nabla n, and derivatives of K with the induced derivative D.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated at the end of Exercise 30.8 after building the induced covariant derivative and extrinsic curvature tensor.
concepts.notes: Foundation of 3+1 (ADM) formulations; not followed up in this chapter.

concepts.name: Bertrand-Diquet-Puiseux theorem
concepts.definition: Gaussian curvature equals the limit as epsilon goes to 0 of (6/epsilon^2)(1 - C/(2 pi epsilon)), where C is the circumference of a geodesic circle of radius epsilon; an area version also exists.
concepts.how_introduced: Exercise 30.3, recalling Exercise 3.3, applied to test a metric for flatness.
concepts.notes: Printed as 'Bertand'.

concepts.name: differential geometry
concepts.definition: The study of curves, surfaces and higher-dimensional spaces using calculus, including their curvature and metric properties.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in the chapter opening as the field founded by applying calculus to geometry.

key_equations.name: Curvature as swept angle per length
key_equations.latex: \kappa(s) = \lim_{\Delta s\to0}\frac{\Delta\theta\ \text{(angle swept by unit tangents on the unit circle)}}{\Delta s\ \text{(arc length on the curve)}}
key_equations.meaning: Operational definition of curvature: map tangents to the unit circle and compare the angle they cover with the distance travelled.
key_equations.symbols: s arc length; theta tangent direction angle

key_equations.name: Curvature of a plane curve
key_equations.meaning: Curvature is the reciprocal radius of the osculating circle and the turning rate of the tangent.

key_equations.name: Curvature from height above tangent line
key_equations.meaning: In coordinates where x runs along the tangent at P, the second derivative of the height equals the curvature.
key_equations.symbols: y height above tangent line; x distance along tangent

key_equations.name: Taylor expansion about P
key_equations.meaning: With y(x_p) = 0 and y'(x_p) = 0 at the tangent point, y = kappa x^2/2, matched to a circle's y ~ x^2/(2 rho).

key_equations.name: Unit tangent
key_equations.meaning: Tangent to a curve given by position vector X(s) in flat 3-space.
key_equations.symbols: X position vector of the curve

key_equations.name: Tangent in a coordinate basis
key_equations.latex: \mathbf t = \frac{d\mathbf X}{ds} = \frac{dx^\mu}{ds}\frac{\partial\mathbf X}{\partial x^\mu} \equiv t^\mu\mathbf e_\mu
key_equations.meaning: Chain rule splits the tangent into components dx^mu/ds and basis vectors dX/dx^mu.

key_equations.name: Principal normal and curvature
key_equations.meaning: Because t has unit length its derivative is perpendicular to it; the direction is p and the magnitude is kappa.

key_equations.name: Chord between unit tangents
key_equations.meaning: Isosceles triangle of unit sides links the vector change of the tangent to the turning angle.

key_equations.name: kappa equals turning rate
key_equations.meaning: Confirms the vector definition agrees with the angle definition (30.9 is the intermediate limit).

key_equations.name: Cyclic triad relations
key_equations.latex: \mathbf b = \mathbf t\times\mathbf p,\quad \mathbf t = \mathbf p\times\mathbf b,\quad \mathbf p = \mathbf b\times\mathbf t
key_equations.meaning: Right-handed orthonormal frame relations used to differentiate p.

key_equations.name: Binormal
key_equations.meaning: Unit normal to the osculating plane.

key_equations.name: Binormal derivative is perpendicular to t
key_equations.latex: \dot{\mathbf b}\cdot\mathbf t = -\mathbf b\cdot\dot{\mathbf t} = -\kappa\,\mathbf b\cdot\mathbf p = 0
key_equations.meaning: Together with b.(db/ds) = 0 this forces db/ds to point along p.

key_equations.name: Torsion
key_equations.meaning: Defines torsion as the rate at which the osculating plane rotates.

key_equations.name: Derivative of principal normal
key_equations.latex: \frac{d\mathbf p}{ds} = \frac{d\mathbf b}{ds}\times\mathbf t + \mathbf b\times\frac{d\mathbf t}{ds} = \tau\mathbf b - \kappa\mathbf t
key_equations.meaning: Obtained by differentiating p = b x t.

key_equations.name: Frenet-Serret equations
key_equations.latex: \frac{d}{ds}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf t\\\mathbf p\\\mathbf b\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0&\kappa&0\\-\kappa&0&\tau\\0&-\tau&0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf t\\\mathbf p\\\mathbf b\end{pmatrix}
key_equations.meaning: A space curve's moving frame rotates with an antisymmetric generator fixed by curvature and torsion alone.

key_equations.name: Surface height as a quadratic form
key_equations.meaning: Near a point, the surface's height above its tangent plane is governed by a symmetric 2x2 curvature tensor.
key_equations.symbols: x^i coordinates in the tangent plane

key_equations.name: Height in matrix form
key_equations.meaning: Same as z = a x^2/2 + b x y + c y^2/2 (30.18).

key_equations.name: Rotation of tangent-plane axes
key_equations.meaning: Choose alpha to diagonalize the symmetric matrix.

key_equations.name: Principal-axis form
key_equations.meaning: In principal axes the height separates; the eigenvalues are the principal curvatures kappa_i = 1/rho_i (matrix form is 30.21).

key_equations.name: General 2D line element
key_equations.meaning: A curved surface uses coordinates with a position-dependent metric; locally flat coordinates give ds^2 = (d\xi^1)^2 + (d\xi^2)^2 (30.23).

key_equations.name: Gauss's formula for K from the metric
key_equations.meaning: Theorema egregium made explicit: Gaussian curvature from metric components and their first and second derivatives only.
key_equations.symbols: commas denote partial derivatives; g = det g_ij (30.26)

key_equations.name: Metric determinant in 2D
key_equations.meaning: Determinant used throughout the intrinsic formulas.

key_equations.name: Gaussian curvature of a sphere
key_equations.meaning: Constant positive curvature of a sphere of radius a; the flat plane gives K = 0 (30.28).

key_equations.name: Gaussian curvature as Gauss-map area ratio
key_equations.latex: K(\mathcal P) = \frac{d\Omega}{dA} = \lim_{\Delta A\to0}\frac{\text{area swept on unit sphere by normals}}{\Delta A\ \text{on the surface}}
key_equations.meaning: Two-dimensional analogue of (30.1).

key_equations.name: Surface basis vectors
key_equations.latex: \mathbf e_1 = \frac{\partial\mathbf X}{\partial x^1},\quad \mathbf e_2 = \frac{\partial\mathbf X}{\partial x^2}
key_equations.meaning: Coordinate tangent vectors of a parametrized surface.

key_equations.name: Unit normal
key_equations.meaning: Normal from the cross product of basis vectors.

key_equations.name: Area element
key_equations.meaning: Area of the coordinate parallelogram on the surface (printed with partial symbols in place of d on the far right).

key_equations.name: Signed area swept by normals
key_equations.latex: d\Omega = \hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\left(\frac{\partial\hat{\mathbf n}}{\partial x^1}\times\frac{\partial\hat{\mathbf n}}{\partial x^2}\right)dx^1dx^2
key_equations.meaning: The cross product of normal derivatives is parallel to n; dotting with n gives a signed solid angle.

key_equations.name: K from unit normal derivatives
key_equations.latex: K = \frac{\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\left(\partial_1\hat{\mathbf n}\times\partial_2\hat{\mathbf n}\right)}{|\mathbf e_1\times\mathbf e_2|}
key_equations.meaning: Computable formula for Gaussian curvature of a parametrized surface.

key_equations.name: Gauss's formula (tangential plus normal split)
key_equations.meaning: Changes of basis vectors have an in-surface part (connection) and an out-of-surface part (second fundamental form).
key_equations.symbols: Gamma connection coefficients; K_mu nu second fundamental form

key_equations.name: Gauss' equation (book's name)
key_equations.meaning: Extract the second fundamental form by projecting basis-vector derivatives onto the normal.

key_equations.name: Cylinder basis and normal
key_equations.meaning: For X = (a cos theta, a sin theta, z) (30.38); only d e_theta/d theta = (-a cos theta, -a sin theta, 0) (30.40) is non-zero, so K_theta theta = -a.

key_equations.name: Split of a surface curve's curvature vector
key_equations.latex: \frac{d\mathbf t}{ds} = \frac{dt^\mu}{ds}\mathbf e_\mu + t^\mu\frac{d\mathbf e_\mu}{ds} = \kappa_g\mathbf e + \kappa_n\hat{\mathbf n}
key_equations.meaning: Curvature of a curve in a surface decomposes into an in-surface (geodesic) part and a normal part; (30.41) is the product-rule step.

key_equations.name: Arc-length derivative via chain rule
key_equations.meaning: Converts derivatives along the curve into surface-coordinate derivatives.

key_equations.name: Normal curvature
key_equations.meaning: The normal curvature depends only on the direction t through the second fundamental form; (30.44) is the projection step.

key_equations.name: First and second fundamental forms
key_equations.latex:
F_1 = g_{\mu
u}dx^\mu dx^
u,\qquad F_2 = K_{\mu
u}dx^\mu dx^
u
key_equations.meaning: Classical names for the line element and the normal-curvature quadratic form (margin note).

key_equations.name: Constrained extremum of normal curvature
key_equations.meaning: Lagrange multiplier k enforces unit tangent length measured by the metric.

key_equations.name: Eigenvalue equation for the shape operator
key_equations.meaning: Principal directions are eigenvectors of A = g^{-1}K; (30.49) is the lowered form K_mu nu t^nu = k g_mu nu t^nu.

key_equations.name: Eigenvalues are extremal normal curvatures
key_equations.meaning: Contracting the eigen-equation with t_lambda (30.54) identifies each eigenvalue with a principal curvature.

key_equations.name: Intrinsic and extrinsic invariants
key_equations.latex: K = \det\underline A = \frac{\det\underline K}{\det\underline g} = k_1k_2,\qquad \mathrm{Tr}\,\underline A = \mathrm{Tr}(\underline g^{-1}\underline K) = k_1+k_2
key_equations.meaning: Determinant is the Gaussian (intrinsic) curvature; trace is what the book calls extrinsic curvature (twice the mean curvature).

key_equations.name: Shape operator of a cylinder
key_equations.meaning: From K = diag(-a, 0) (30.51) and inverse metric diag(1/a^2, 1) (30.52): K = 0, trace -1/a.

key_equations.name: Paraboloid metric
key_equations.meaning: Induced metric of X = (x, y, u x^2/2 + v y^2/2) (30.56); at the origin it is the identity and K_11 = u, K_22 = v.

key_equations.name: Sphere basis-vector derivatives (corrected)
key_equations.latex: \partial_\theta\mathbf e_\theta = -a\hat{\mathbf n},\quad \partial_\phi\mathbf e_\theta = \partial_\theta\mathbf e_\phi = \cot\theta\,\mathbf e_\phi,\quad \partial_\phi\mathbf e_\phi = -\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\mathbf e_\theta - a\sin^2\theta\,\hat{\mathbf n}
key_equations.meaning: Normal parts give K_theta theta = -a, K_phi phi = -a sin^2 theta; tangential parts are the familiar sphere Christoffel symbols. The printed version has a spurious factor a in both tangential terms.
key_equations.symbols: X = a(sin theta cos phi, sin theta sin phi, cos theta) (30.62)

key_equations.name: Gaussian curvature from Riemann in 2D
key_equations.meaning: In two dimensions the single independent Riemann component divided by the metric determinant is Gauss's curvature.

key_equations.name: R_1212 from the metric
key_equations.meaning: Specialization of eqn 11.22 used to check (30.65) against (30.25).

key_equations.name: Sample Christoffel symbol (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: From the standard formula (30.67). The printed version omits the factor 1/2 and writes g_{21,1} where g_{21,2} is needed.

key_equations.name: 2x2 inverse metric (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Needed for the verification in Example 30.11. The printed line gives g^22 = g_22/g and appends '= g_21/g' to g^12, both errors.

key_equations.name: Circumference-deficit curvature (Exercise 30.3)
key_equations.meaning: Intrinsic measurement of K from geodesic circles.

key_equations.name: Weingarten's equation (Exercise 30.5)
key_equations.meaning: Second fundamental form from how the normal tilts; equivalent to (30.37) since e_mu . n = 0.

key_equations.name: Extrinsic curvature tensor of a hypersurface (Exercise 30.8)
key_equations.meaning: Covariant generalization of the second fundamental form for a spacelike hypersurface with unit normal n; (30.83)-(30.84) define P and h.
key_equations.symbols: P projector; n timelike unit normal

key_equations.name: Gauss equation for a hypersurface
key_equations.latex: P^\mu{}_\alpha P^\nu{}_\beta P^\sigma{}_\gamma P^\rho{}_\delta R_{\mu\nu\sigma\rho} = {}^{(3)}R_{\alpha\beta\gamma\delta} - K_{\alpha\delta}K_{\beta\gamma} + K_{\alpha\gamma}K_{\beta\delta}
key_equations.meaning: Projected spacetime curvature equals intrinsic curvature of the slice plus products of extrinsic curvature: the higher-dimensional heir of K = det K/det g.

key_equations.name: Codazzi equation
key_equations.latex: P^\mu{}_\alpha P^\nu{}_\beta P^\sigma{}_\gamma n^\rho R_{\mu\nu\sigma\rho} = D_\beta K_{\alpha\gamma} - D_\alpha K_{\beta\gamma}
key_equations.meaning: Mixed normal-tangential projection of Riemann is governed by derivatives of extrinsic curvature.

figures.label: Fig. 30.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: The edge of a guitar body is a path in the plane; its tight upper bend (radius rho_1) is more curved than the gentler lower bend (radius rho_2).
figures.visual_description: Greyscale photo of the left half of an electric guitar body seen from the front (pickups and bridge visible at right). Along the upper waist, three arrows drawn tangent to the outline fan out sharply from a small region, with lines to a nearby centre labelled rho_1 creating a small sector. Along the lower bout, several tangent arrows with small right-angle marks show normals converging to a centre well inside the body, drawn as a larger triangle labelled rho_2.
figures.what_it_teaches: Curvature varies along a curve and is judged by how quickly tangent directions change; a smaller best-fit radius means greater curvature.

redesign.idea: Drive-the-curve: a car moves along an editable spline outline (default a guitar body); a steering-wheel gauge and a live osculating circle show curvature, and a strip chart plots kappa(s).
redesign.interaction: Drag spline control points; scrub or play the car along the curve; toggle display of tangent arrows, normals, centre of curvature trace (evolute).

figures.label: Fig. 30.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: At a point P on a wavy curve, the best-fitting circle has centre C and radius rho.
figures.visual_description: A black wavy line runs left to right with a trough near the middle. A circle sits in the trough touching the curve at a point labelled P (calligraphic) with a small right-angle mark. Inside the circle a dot marks the centre C, joined to P by a short arrowed segment labelled rho.
figures.what_it_teaches: Curvature at a point is the reciprocal radius of the circle that kisses the curve there, centred along the normal.

redesign.idea: Two-normals construction: draw normals at P and at a second point Q; their intersection converges to the centre of curvature as Q slides toward P, and the osculating circle snaps in.
redesign.interaction: Drag Q along the curve toward P; drag P; readout of rho and kappa, with a ghost circle through three nearby points for comparison.

figures.label: Fig. 30.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Arc-length parametrization labels points by distance measured along the curve.
figures.visual_description: A thick S-shaped curve climbs from lower left to upper right, marked with evenly spaced cross ticks; the first five are labelled s1 to s5 near the lower bend. Beneath the flatter middle and right part of the curve runs a dotted line that roughly follows it, hinting that a curve can be traced with other, unevenly spaced parameters.
figures.what_it_teaches: The parameter s is physical distance along the curve, which makes tangent vectors unit length.

redesign.idea: Side-by-side parametrizations: the same curve with ticks at equal parameter steps for an arbitrary lambda versus equal arc length, with tangent arrows whose lengths show speed.
redesign.interaction: Switch parametrization; slide a spacing slider; watch tangent lengths become uniform under arc length.

figures.label: Fig. 30.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: Unit tangents along a stretch of curve of length Delta s (top) are transplanted to a unit circle, where they span an angle Delta theta (bottom).
figures.visual_description: Upper left: a curve rising to the right with unit tangent arrows at three dots; a parallel arc beside it is labelled Delta s. Lower right: a circle with several arrows from its centre to the rim, fanning out by an angle labelled Delta theta at the centre.
figures.what_it_teaches: Curvature is the ratio of turning angle on the tangent indicatrix to arc length travelled; this ratio is the template later upgraded to solid angle per area.

redesign.idea: Linked tangent indicatrix: as a highlighted segment of the curve grows, its unit tangents are copied to a unit circle and the swept arc and Delta theta/Delta s ratio update; later tab shows the surface version with normals painting a patch on a sphere.
redesign.interaction: Drag the segment endpoints; shrink Delta s to see the ratio converge to kappa; switch to surface mode to paint the Gauss map.

figures.label: Fig. 30.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: At a point of a space curve X(s) the tangent t, principal normal p and binormal b = t x p form a triad; t and p span the osculating plane.
figures.visual_description: A thick curve labelled X(s) rises diagonally, dotted at both ends. At a point on it three arrows emerge: t along the curve to the upper right, p to the left, b straight up. A dashed wireframe box is drawn on these edges, with the vertical face between p and b hatched diagonally and another face stippled, suggesting planes attached to the frame.
figures.what_it_teaches: A space curve carries a moving orthonormal frame; bending happens in the t-p plane, twisting is rotation of that plane about t.

redesign.idea: Frenet frame rider on a helix or knot in 3D: a translucent osculating plane and osculating circle ride along; sliders set constant kappa and tau and the curve is rebuilt by integrating the Frenet-Serret equations.
redesign.interaction: Orbit camera; scrub s; set kappa(s), tau(s) (constants or drawn profiles); toggle ribbon showing b to visualize twist; set tau = 0 to see a planar circle.

figures.label: Fig. 30.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: A bowl-shaped surface touches a tangent plane; curvature at a point is judged by the surface's height z above that plane.
figures.visual_description: A shaded paraboloid bowl opening upward, its lowest point resting on a flat parallelogram labelled 'tangent plane' with a curly pointer. A vertical arrow rises from the contact point. A dashed horizontal line and a point P on the bowl's side, with a double-headed vertical arrow labelled z from the plane up to the level of P; an axis arrow labelled x runs to the right in the plane.
figures.what_it_teaches: Near a point, a surface is a quadratic height function over its tangent plane whose coefficients encode curvature in every direction.

redesign.idea: Quadric sculptor: a 3D patch z = (1/2)(a x^2 + 2b x y + c y^2) over its tangent plane, with the Dupin indicatrix drawn on the plane and principal axes that rotate as the learner changes b; a normal-section plane sweeps around showing kappa_n(phi).
redesign.interaction: Sliders for a, b, c (allowing saddles); rotate a slicing plane about the normal and watch the section curve and its osculating circle; readouts of eigenvalues, K and k1 + k2.

figures.label: Fig. 30.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: A curve drawn on a curved sheet passes through a point P.
figures.visual_description: Hand-drawn wavy sheet like a draped cloth, higher at the back corners with hatching for shading. A black curve runs from the front-left across the sheet to the back-right, with a dot on it labelled P.
figures.what_it_teaches: Curves living in a surface inherit bending from the surface (normal curvature) plus their own sideways bending within it.

redesign.idea: Curvature vector split: on a 3D surface, the learner draws a curve through P; the acceleration vector dt/ds appears with its normal component (kappa_n) and in-surface component (kappa_g) shown as coloured arrows.
redesign.interaction: Draw or drag the curve direction at P; rotate direction through 360 degrees to see kappa_n trace Euler's cos^2 law; snap to the geodesic to make kappa_g vanish.

figures.label: Fig. 30.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: A tin can wrapped in a grid looks curved but has zero intrinsic curvature; the same grid sheet lies flat beside it. For radius a the eigenvalues are -1/a and 0, so K = 0 while k1 + k2 = -1/a.
figures.visual_description: Rendered 3D scene: a ring-pull can standing on a patterned surface, its side covered by square grid paper with handwritten text 'surface looks curved'. In front lies a flat rectangular grid sheet; left part reads 'surface looks curved', right part '...but it is not intrinsically curved!'. Soft shadows and a swirl-patterned floor. The inventory gives no label for this image; it is Fig. 30.8.
figures.what_it_teaches: Bending without stretching changes extrinsic curvature but not intrinsic curvature; a cylinder is intrinsically flat.

redesign.idea: Roll and unroll: a grid sheet morphs continuously between flat, cylinder and cone, with a triangle of geodesics drawn on it whose angle sum stays 180 degrees; a second sheet is forced onto a sphere and visibly tears or wrinkles, with angle sum exceeding 180.
redesign.interaction: Slider for roll amount; toggle cylinder, cone, sphere targets; readouts of k1, k2, K and k1 + k2 at a probe point.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.1
worked_examples.problem: Find an alternative, parametrization-based definition of curvature and check it on a circle.
worked_examples.method: Parametrize by arc length; transplant unit tangents from a short stretch onto a unit circle; divide the swept angle by the arc length and take the limit. For a circle of radius rho, arc length rho times the angle gives the ratio directly.
worked_examples.key_insight: Curvature is a turning rate: angle of tangent change per distance travelled.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.2
worked_examples.problem: Justify that the second derivative of height above the tangent line equals the curvature.
worked_examples.method: Taylor-expand y about x_p with the tangent line as x-axis so the constant and linear terms vanish, giving y = kappa x^2/2. Compare with the height rho(1 - cos theta) of a tangent circle, which for small theta = x/rho is x^2/(2 rho).
worked_examples.key_insight: Locally every smooth curve looks like a parabola whose coefficient is half the curvature; the circle and the parabola agree to second order.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.3
worked_examples.problem: Show that the coefficient kappa in dt/ds = kappa p is the same curvature as d(theta)/ds.
worked_examples.method: The change between two unit tangents is the base of an isosceles triangle with unit sides, of length 2 sin(Delta theta/2) which is Delta theta to third order; divide by Delta s and take the limit, using |p| = 1.
worked_examples.key_insight: For unit vectors, the size of a small change equals the small angle turned.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.4
worked_examples.problem: Determine the direction of the derivative of the binormal.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate b.b = 1 to get b.(db/ds) = 0 (printed with the dot missing). Differentiate b.t = 0 and use dt/ds = kappa p and b.p = 0 to get (db/ds).t = 0. Being perpendicular to both b and t, db/ds lies along p.
worked_examples.key_insight: Orthonormality constraints, differentiated, restrict which directions a frame vector can move in; this is why the Frenet matrix is antisymmetric.
worked_examples.result: db/ds is parallel to p, motivating db/ds = -tau p

worked_examples.label: Example 30.5
worked_examples.problem: Reduce the general quadratic height z = a x^2/2 + b x y + c y^2/2 of a surface above its tangent plane to principal form, and apply it to a sphere of radius a resting on a plane.
worked_examples.method: Write z as a symmetric matrix quadratic form, rotate axes by an angle alpha chosen to diagonalize, giving z = kappa_1 xi^2/2 + kappa_2 eta^2/2. For the sphere, expand the lower hemisphere's height near the contact point to second order.
worked_examples.key_insight: Principal curvatures are eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix and principal directions are its perpendicular eigenvectors.
worked_examples.result: Sphere: both principal curvatures equal 1/a. Printed errors: the height is written with (a^2 + x^2 + y^2)^{1/2} instead of a - (a^2 - x^2 - y^2)^{1/2}, and the expansion coefficient appears as 1/(2a^2) where 1/(2a) is needed for kappa = 1/a.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.6
worked_examples.problem: Exhibit Gauss's intrinsic curvature as a function of the metric and test it on a sphere and a plane.
worked_examples.method: Assume locally Euclidean coordinates exist at a point but not over a region; write the general line element g_ij dx^i dx^j; present Gauss's formula (30.25) involving g, its first and second derivatives and determinant g; substitute g_theta theta = a^2, g_phi phi = a^2 sin^2 theta, and the flat metric.
worked_examples.key_insight: Curvature can be computed from distances alone, although the explicit formula is unwieldy, motivating better tools.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.7
worked_examples.problem: Turn the area-swept-by-normals definition of Gaussian curvature into a formula in terms of a surface parametrization.
worked_examples.method: Build the unit normal from e_1 x e_2; the surface area element is |e_1 x e_2| dx^1 dx^2; the image area on the unit sphere comes from the cross product of the normal's coordinate derivatives, made signed by dotting with n; divide.
worked_examples.key_insight: Gaussian curvature is the Jacobian of the Gauss map. Dotting with n also makes it harmless to ignore the derivative of the normalization factor, since that term is along n and drops out of the triple product.
worked_examples.result: K = n.(d_1 n x d_2 n)/|e_1 x e_2|

worked_examples.label: Example 30.8
worked_examples.problem: Compute the second fundamental form of a cylinder of radius a.
worked_examples.method: Parametrize X = (a cos theta, a sin theta, z); find e_theta, e_z and outward unit normal; differentiate the basis vectors; only d e_theta/d theta is non-zero; project on n.
worked_examples.key_insight: Straight generators contribute nothing to K_mu nu; all bending is around the circumference.
worked_examples.result: K_theta theta = -a, other components zero; metric g_theta theta = a^2, g_zz = 1.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.9
worked_examples.problem: Find the extreme values of the normal curvature K_mu nu t^mu t^nu over all unit tangent directions at a point.
worked_examples.method: Lagrange multiplier k with constraint g_mu nu t^mu t^nu = 1; differentiate with respect to t^mu; raise an index with the inverse metric to get an eigenvalue equation for A = g^{-1}K; contract with t_lambda to identify each eigenvalue with the extremal normal curvature. Margin note: for the cylinder A = diag(-1/a, 0).
worked_examples.key_insight: The metric enters because 'unit length' on a curved surface is measured by g, so the relevant matrix is g^{-1}K, not K.
worked_examples.result: Eigenvalues k_1, k_2 of g^{lambda mu}K_mu nu are the principal curvatures; det and trace are invariants.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.10
worked_examples.problem: Compute intrinsic (det) and extrinsic (trace) curvatures for (a) the paraboloid z = u x^2/2 + v y^2/2 at its vertex and (b) a sphere of radius a.
worked_examples.method: (a) Find e_x, e_y, metric (30.57), unit normal and second derivatives of X; at the origin g is the identity and K = diag(u, v). (b) Use spherical parametrization, basis vectors, outward normal; decompose second derivatives into tangential and normal parts to read K_11 = -a, K_22 = -a sin^2 theta; combine with g = diag(a^2, a^2 sin^2 theta).
worked_examples.key_insight: Determinant of g^{-1}K reproduces Gauss's intrinsic value; the trace depends on the normal orientation and embedding.
worked_examples.result: (a) K = uv, trace u + v. (b) K = 1/a^2, trace -2/a. Printed slips: the origin metric is labelled g_uu, g_vv, g_uv (should be g_xx, g_yy, g_xy); in (30.64) the tangential terms carry a spurious factor a.

worked_examples.label: Example 30.11
worked_examples.problem: Justify K = R_1212/g by checking it against Gauss's metric formula.
worked_examples.method: Write 4gR_1212 = 4g^2 K; expand R_1212 using eqn 11.22; compute Christoffel symbols from the metric formula; use the explicit 2x2 inverse metric; compare term by term with (30.25). The algebra is left to the reader.
worked_examples.key_insight: Gauss's ugly formula is just the one independent Riemann component in 2D, divided by det g.
worked_examples.result: Claimed agreement (not carried out). Printed errors in the supporting equations: (30.68) lacks 1/2 and has g_{21,1} for g_{21,2}; (30.69) has g^22 = g_22/g instead of g_11/g and a wrong sign in '= g_21/g'.

worked_examples.problem: Count the number of functions in a metric that carry genuine geometric information (Riemann's argument, with margin note 24).
worked_examples.method: A symmetric n x n matrix has n diagonal entries and half of n^2 - n off-diagonal ones, total n(n+1)/2; subtract the n functions available in choosing coordinates.
worked_examples.key_insight: Coordinate freedom removes n functions; what remains must be curvature-like data.
worked_examples.result: n(n-1)/2 functions (1 for a surface, 3 in 3D, 6 in 4D).
concepts: degrees of freedom of a metric

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Driving a car around the bends of a road shaped like a guitar outline: the harder you turn the steering wheel at constant speed, the greater the curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives a bodily sense of curvature as turning rate before introducing the circle yardstick.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Steering angle relates to curvature only at fixed speed and fixed wheelbase geometry; says nothing about surfaces or intrinsic curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Car on an editable road with a steering-wheel dial that rotates in proportion to kappa.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The osculating circle as the circle that kisses the curve (Latin osculum).
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Etymology in a margin note to fix the image of second-order contact.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: A kiss suggests touching, which a tangent line also does; the circle's special feature is matching curvature too.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Locally every curve is a parabola and every surface is a quadratic bowl or saddle over its tangent plane.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Margin note 5 notes the coordinate method really compares with a parabola; the idea is carried to z = K_ij x^i x^j/2.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Second-order only; higher terms matter for how curvature varies from point to point.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Zoom slider on a surface patch that progressively overlays the best-fit quadric until they are indistinguishable.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Ellipse with major and minor axes as the 2D generalization of the circle used to gauge curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates two curvature numbers in perpendicular directions via Euler's result.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The level curve of the quadratic form is an ellipse only when both curvatures share a sign; saddles give hyperbolas; its semi-axes scale as rho_i^{1/2}, not as the curvatures themselves.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Dupin indicatrix drawn on the tangent plane that morphs from circle to ellipse to parabola pair to hyperbola as curvature parameters change.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Beings confined to a surface who cannot jump out to look at its shape.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames Gauss's goal of an insider-measurable curvature and Riemann's extension to our own space.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Leaves open how inhabitants actually measure it; the book supplies formulas rather than insider experiments (exercises add loops and circles).
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: First-person ant view on a hidden surface: the learner pays out string to measure circle circumferences and infers K before the surface is revealed.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Unit tangents on a circle for curves become unit normals painting a patch on a sphere for surfaces.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Defines K as swept solid angle per area by direct analogy with swept angle per length.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Needs an embedding to define normals, so it does not by itself show intrinsicness.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Brush a region on a surface and watch its normal image fill in on a companion sphere, with area ratio readout and orientation reversal on saddles.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A tin can wrapped in a flat grid sheet: it looks curved but the paper lies flat once unwrapped, whereas paper cannot cover a sphere without cutting.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Separates bending visible from outside from curvature inherent to the surface (Fig. 30.8).
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Suggests extrinsic curvature is illusory; it is physically real (e.g. for embedded hypersurfaces in GR) just not detectable from within.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph flat sheet into cylinder while tracking a drawn triangle's angles and edge lengths, then attempt a sphere.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Shoelaces, however tangled, can be pulled straight.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Explains why a one-dimensional curve has only extrinsic curvature.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Pulling straight preserves length, which is the point; a learner may wrongly generalize that any surface can be smoothed out likewise.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A curve has intrinsic curvature just as a surface does.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A 1D space can always be laid out straight without stretching; its curvature is purely extrinsic. Intrinsic curvature needs at least two dimensions.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter spends two sections on curvature of lines, and it is the same word.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A cylinder is a curved surface in the same sense as a sphere.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Its Gaussian curvature is zero (k1 = -1/a, k2 = 0); only its extrinsic curvature is non-zero.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: It visibly bends when seen from outside.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A surface's curvature can be captured by one number or by one comparison sphere.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Bending generally differs by direction; two principal curvatures in perpendicular directions are needed, from which K and the trace are formed.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The curve story needed only one circle.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Metric components that vary with position mean the space is curved.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The g_ij depend on the coordinates chosen; only coordinate-independent combinations such as K or the Riemann tensor signal curvature (e.g. polar coordinates on a flat plane).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Curved-space examples always come with non-constant metrics.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The eigenvalues of K_mu nu itself are the principal curvatures.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Unless coordinates are orthonormal at the point, the relevant matrix is g^{-1}K; e.g. for the cylinder K_theta theta = -a but the curvature is -1/a.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Example 30.5 tangent-plane coordinates are orthonormal, so K alone worked there.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Extrinsic curvature is not physical, so it is irrelevant for general relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Spacetime itself is not embedded, but surfaces and hypersurfaces within spacetime (spatial slices, horizons) have extrinsic curvature that enters the Gauss-Codazzi equations and 3+1 formulations, as Exercises 30.7-30.8 preview.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The chapter emphasizes that inhabitants cannot see the embedding and that intrinsic curvature is what matters for GR.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Torsion of a curve is the same torsion as in torsion-free connections.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Curve torsion measures twisting of the Frenet frame of one curve in flat space; connection torsion is an antisymmetric part of the connection, a different object.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Same word, both about twisting, and GA later assumes torsion-free connections.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The sign of principal curvatures of a sphere is intrinsically negative (as Example 30.10 gives -1/a).
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The signs of K_mu nu and k_i flip with the choice of normal direction; their product K = k1 k2 does not.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The examples present signed values without comment.

thought_experiments.name: Flatlanders measuring their own curvature
thought_experiments.setup: Two-dimensional beings confined to a surface can measure lengths and angles but cannot leave the surface to view it from outside.
thought_experiments.lesson: A useful notion of curvature for physics must be computable from internal measurements, which Gauss achieved for surfaces and Riemann for any dimension; we are in the same position with respect to spacetime.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Hidden-surface game: learner measures circle circumferences or triangle angle sums from inside and must guess sphere, plane, cylinder or saddle.

thought_experiments.name: Unwrapping a tin can versus wrapping a ball
thought_experiments.setup: Peel the label off a cylinder and lay it flat; then try to cover a sphere with flat paper.
thought_experiments.lesson: Surfaces that unroll have no intrinsic curvature; a sphere forces cutting or stretching, revealing intrinsic curvature.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Physics-based cloth sheet that can wrap a cylinder cleanly but wrinkles on a sphere, with a stretch heat map.

thought_experiments.name: Parallel transport around a loop on a sphere
thought_experiments.setup: Carry a vector around a closed loop on a 2-sphere and compare its final direction with the initial one (Exercise 30.2).
thought_experiments.lesson: The rotation angle divided by enclosed area equals the Gaussian curvature 1/a^2, an internal measurement.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Drag a loop on a sphere; an arrow is parallel-transported around it; angle vs area plotted to show a straight line of slope 1/a^2.

historical_notes.event: Grossmann introduced his friend Einstein to differential geometry when Einstein began building general relativity.
historical_notes.significance: Reassures physics readers that unfamiliarity with this mathematics is normal.

historical_notes.event: Development of curvature of curves by applying calculus to geometry, including the osculating-circle construction followed in 30.1.
The moving-frame equations appear in Frenet's 1847 thesis (abstract published 1852) and were published independently by Serret in 1851.
historical_notes.significance: Explains the dual naming Frenet-Serret or Serret-Frenet.

historical_notes.event: Euler showed that the directions of maximal and minimal normal curvature of a surface are perpendicular.
historical_notes.significance: Reduces surface curvature at a point to two numbers; a margin note records Gauss's high praise of Euler's works.

historical_notes.event: Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas establishes intrinsic Gaussian curvature and the theorema egregium.
historical_notes.significance: First proof that curvature can be measured from within a surface.

historical_notes.event: Habilitation lecture at Gottingen setting out a programme for curvature of n-dimensional spaces with minimal mathematics. The book dates it 1853 (the year the lecture topic was set); it was delivered in June 1854, as GA ch11 itself states.
historical_notes.significance: Conceptual foundation for the geometry of general relativity.

historical_notes.event: Paris Academy prize essay on heat conduction contains the first explicit curvature tensor in terms of the metric and the flatness criterion; Riemann, in poor health, did not win for lack of detail, and the prize was withdrawn in 1868.

applications_and_observations.topic: Numerical checks of curvature for standard shapes
applications_and_observations.details: Sphere radius a: principal curvatures magnitude 1/a, K = 1/a^2, trace magnitude 2/a. Cylinder radius a: k = -1/a and 0, K = 0. Paraboloid vertex: K = uv, trace u + v. Our own illustration: for the Earth (a about 6371 km), K is about 2.5e-14 per square metre, so a geodesic triangle of area 1e6 km^2 has angle excess about 0.025 rad (1.4 degrees).

Exercises 30.7-30.8 build projection operators, induced metric, induced covariant derivative and extrinsic curvature tensor for a spacelike slice, ending with the Gauss and Codazzi equations. These underpin the constraint equations of numerical relativity (not discussed in the chapter; context added by us).

notation_and_conventions.convention: Bold letters denote vectors in flat three-dimensional embedding space; described as a temporary measure for this chapter.
From Example 30.3 on, an overdot means d/ds.
t tangent, p principal normal, b binormal (many texts use T, N, B).

K_ij or K_mu nu is the second fundamental form (curvature tensor of the height quadric); unsubscripted K is Gaussian curvature; in Exercise 30.8 K_alpha beta is the spacetime extrinsic curvature tensor.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Easy to confuse with the trace K = K^mu_mu common in GR literature.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Underlined bold letters (A, K, g) denote matrices of components; A = g^{-1}K.
notation_and_conventions.notes: In margin note 20 the matrix labelled g holds inverse-metric components g^{lambda mu}, while elsewhere det g is the determinant of the metric itself.

notation_and_conventions.convention: g_{12,12} means the second partial derivative of g_12 with respect to x^1 and x^2.

Unit normal n = e_1 x e_2/|e_1 x e_2|; for the cylinder and sphere this is outward, giving negative K_mu nu and principal curvatures; for the paraboloid it points up into the bowl giving positive values.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Sign of the trace depends on this choice; K does not.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The book calls the trace k1 + k2 the extrinsic curvature (standard: twice the mean curvature).
3Q(X,Y) = -R(X,Y,X,Y) with R the (0,4) tensor; K = R_1212/g in 2D, consistent with GA's MTW-type sign convention (R_{theta phi theta phi} = a^2 sin^2 theta for a sphere).
P^mu_nu = delta^mu_nu + n^mu n_nu for a timelike unit normal presumes n.n = -1, i.e. the book's (-,+,+,+) signature.

margin_notes.summary: Chapter is called classical to contrast with the coordinate-free approach of later chapters and may be skipped.
Chapter epigraph: a tongue-in-cheek remark by John Dalton about a paper interesting to those interested in it.
Osculate derives from the Latin for kiss.
Length parametrization was covered in Chapter 9; normals are tangents rotated by a right angle.
The coordinate method really compares the curve with a parabola of constant second derivative; this idea returns for surfaces.
Using a position vector X depends on the flat 3D embedding and will not be attempted for curved spacetime.
Frenet and Serret biographies and the tangled priority history of their equations.
Euler biography with Gauss's praise of Euler's works as the best school of mathematics.
Gauss's 1827 paper and Spivak's Volume II, which translates it with a modern commentary, recommended.
Egregium originally meant remarkable; Fowler's usage guide on the modern pejorative sense of egregious.
Needham (2021) recommended for making the theorema egregium intuitive with several proofs.
Surface coordinates play the role that s played for curves.
When differentiating the unit normal, the normalization factor 1/|n| is treated as a constant.
Gauss has so many equations that the label Gauss' equation is ambiguous.
Cylinder metric components g_theta theta = a^2, g_zz = 1 recorded for later use.
First and second fundamental forms defined, with the remark that the terminology will not be used.
The unit-length constraint needs the metric because the surface is curved; worked cylinder matrices K, inverse g and A.
One-dimensional curves have no intrinsic curvature: shoelaces can always be laid straight.
Sphere metric, determinant a^4 sin^2 theta, and inverse metric.
Riemann's Gottingen inaugural lecture was aimed at the whole faculty; its significance is discussed in Spivak Vol. II.
Derivation that a symmetric metric has n(n+1)/2 independent components; Q is a function of two vectors spanning a plane W.
Riemann's 1861 prize entry failed for lack of detail and the prize was withdrawn; explicit relation 3Q(X,Y) = -R(X,Y,X,Y); Spivak for details.
