notable.summary: Show that curvature equals the sideways force needed to keep a unit mass moving at unit speed along a planar curve.
notable.why_notable: Links geometry to Newtonian mechanics and foreshadows acceleration of world lines.

notable.summary: Use the rotation of a parallel-transported vector around a loop divided by the loop area to get Gaussian curvature 1/a^2 on a sphere.
notable.why_notable: An insider's measurement of K, bridging to holonomy and the Riemann tensor of ch11 and ch35.

notable.summary: Apply the circumference-deficit formula for K to the metric dr^2 + sin^2 r dtheta^2 to decide whether it is flat.
notable.why_notable: Concrete insider test; the metric is the unit sphere so K = 1.

notable.summary: Write the eigen-equation as a characteristic determinant and show the determinant and trace of g^{-1}K give the product and sum of the eigenvalues.
notable.why_notable: Fills in the linear algebra behind the intrinsic/extrinsic split.

notable.summary: Derive Weingarten's equation by differentiating the orthogonality of tangent and normal, then use it to show K = det K / det g.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the missing proof that the determinant of the shape operator equals the Gauss-map area ratio.

notable.summary: Redo the paraboloid of Example 30.10 at a general point three ways: Gauss's equation, Weingarten's equation and the normal-sweep formula.
notable.why_notable: Away from the vertex the metric is not the identity, forcing proper use of g^{-1}K.

notable.summary: For a spacelike hypersurface with timelike unit normal, show the projector is idempotent, projects vectors into the surface, and induces a spatial metric.
notable.why_notable: First step into 3+1 geometry used in numerical relativity.

notable.summary: Build the induced covariant derivative, show it is compatible with the induced metric, define the extrinsic curvature tensor and split the spacetime derivative into tangential and normal parts; the Gauss and Codazzi equations are then quoted.
notable.why_notable: Covariant generalization of eqn 30.36 to hypersurfaces in spacetime.

exercises.solutions: GA has an Appendix E of answers to selected problems; whether it covers any ch30 exercise was not checked.

difficulty.notes: Curves (30.1-30.2) are gentle calculus and vector algebra. Surfaces demand comfort with index notation, eigenproblems with a non-trivial metric and many small typos to navigate. Gauss's formula is displayed, not derived; the key claim that det(g^{-1}K) is intrinsic is asserted. Section 30.6 is historical and qualitative. Exercises 30.7-30.8 are a jump in sophistication (covariant derivatives on hypersurfaces). Several printed errors (sphere height, 30.25 sign, 30.64 factors, 30.68-30.69) will frustrate careful readers.

teaching_gems.gem: One ratio, two dimensions: curvature of a curve is angle swept by unit tangents per length; Gaussian curvature is solid angle swept by unit normals per area.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Learners reuse a picture they already understand, and the definition is visual and computable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Split screen: curve with tangent circle on the left, surface with normal sphere on the right; brushing a segment or patch paints its image and shows the ratio live.

teaching_gems.gem: Local shape as a Taylor expansion over the tangent line or plane, with curvature read off as the quadratic coefficient.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an abstract notion into 'the second derivative', and makes principal curvatures an eigenvalue problem students have met.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Sliders for a, b, c of a quadric patch with its principal axes and Dupin indicatrix updating; saddle regime highlighted.

teaching_gems.gem: Split derivatives of basis vectors into a part inside the surface and a part sticking out.
teaching_gems.why_effective: The tangential part previews the connection and the normal part defines extrinsic curvature; the same decomposition returns in hypersurface GR.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Move along a coordinate line on a sphere; the change of e_theta is drawn as an arrow decomposed into coloured tangential (Gamma) and normal (K) components.

teaching_gems.gem: Tin can versus ball: a grid sheet wraps a cylinder and lies flat again, but cannot cover a sphere.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A kitchen-table demonstration that separates looking curved from being curved.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Roll-and-unroll animation with geodesic triangle angle sums and a wrinkle/stretch map on the sphere attempt.

teaching_gems.gem: Determinant versus trace of g^{-1}K as the intrinsic versus extrinsic invariants, checked on a cylinder (0 and -1/a).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Compact algebraic criterion that matches the physical intuition; the cylinder is a perfect counterexample to 'looks curved'.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Surface gallery (plane, cylinder, cone, sphere, saddle, torus) with a probe showing k1, k2, product and sum; bend a sheet and watch the sum change while the product stays fixed.

teaching_gems.gem: Showing Gauss's full metric formula to dramatize how hard intrinsic curvature is by brute force.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Motivates later efficient machinery (Riemann tensor, Cartan) and makes the theorema egregium feel genuinely remarkable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Symbolic calculator: learner enters a 2D metric; the app evaluates K by Gauss's formula, by R_1212/g and by Brioschi form, showing they agree.

teaching_gems.gem: Frenet-Serret as an antisymmetric matrix acting on a moving frame.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Antisymmetry follows from orthonormality and prepares for rotation generators and connection one-forms in Cartan's method.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draw kappa(s) and tau(s) as graphs; the app integrates the frame to build the 3D curve in real time.

teaching_gems.gem: Shoelaces can always be pulled straight, so curves have no intrinsic curvature.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Instantly explains why intrinsic curvature needs two or more dimensions.
teaching_gems.app_idea: A tangled 3D string that straightens while preserving its length, with tick marks staying equally spaced.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Section 30.1 first says the upper bend of the guitar is more curved (consistent with Fig. 30.1, where rho_1 at the top is small), then states the bottom feature has the smaller osculating radius.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Contradiction on the very first example may shake confidence in kappa = 1/rho.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State clearly: the tight top bend has smaller radius and larger curvature.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Sphere example in 30.3: height printed with a^2 + x^2 + y^2 under the root and expansion coefficient 1/(2a^2); correct is z = a - (a^2 - x^2 - y^2)^{1/2} which is approximately (x^2 + y^2)/(2a).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The printed coefficient would give curvature 1/a^2, contradicting the stated 1/a.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected expansion and point out dimensional analysis (z must have units of length).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The ellipse description of principal curvatures is loose: the book says eigenvalues give the ellipse axes and inverse eigenvalues the curvatures, contradicting eqn 30.22 where eigenvalues are the curvatures; for saddles the level set is a hyperbola.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion about whether K_ij eigenvalues are curvatures or radii.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Say eigenvalues are principal curvatures; the level set K_ij x^i x^j = 1 (Dupin indicatrix) has semi-axes 1/sqrt(kappa_i).

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Eqn 30.25 as printed drops a minus sign inside the second factor of the product in the g_12 bracket: that factor should be the difference 2 g_{12,2} minus g_{22,1}, but it is typeset as a product of the two terms.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Anyone checking a metric with off-diagonal terms gets a wrong K.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected formula in the dossier, or better, compute K via R_1212/g or Brioschi's formula.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The central claim that det(g^{-1}K) is the intrinsic Gaussian curvature is introduced with 'it turns out'; the chain from Gauss-map ratio to det K/det g (Exercise 30.5) and from there to the metric formula (theorema egregium proper) is not shown.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: The key conceptual surprise, that an extrinsically defined product is intrinsic, is accepted on authority.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the Gauss equation R_1212 = K_11 K_22 - K_12^2 for a surface (a 2D instance of eqn 30.89) using Gauss's formula for basis derivatives and commuting partial derivatives, which makes intrinsicness evident.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Example 30.4 prints 'b.b = 0' where b.(db/ds) = 0 is meant; the text also says b measures the rate of change of the osculating plane when db/ds (i.e. tau) does.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Momentary confusion over a contradiction with b.b = 1.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write the derivative explicitly and attribute twisting to tau.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Errors in worked details: eqn 30.64 tangential terms carry a spurious factor a (should be cot theta e_phi and -sin theta cos theta e_theta); Example 30.10 labels metric components g_uu, g_vv with the parameter names; eqn 30.68 misses 1/2 and has g_{21,1} for g_{21,2}; eqn 30.69 gives g^22 = g_22/g (should be g_11/g) and appends a wrong-sign '= g_21/g'.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers attempting the 'try it and see' verification in Example 30.11 will fail.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide corrected formulas and a worked verification for a diagonal metric such as the sphere.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Margin note 15 tells readers not to differentiate the normalization of n without saying why that is legitimate.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Looks like an unjustified shortcut; applied elsewhere it would be wrong.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain that the extra term is along n and drops out of both n.(d_1 n x d_2 n) and e_mu . d_nu n.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: kappa_g is introduced but never named or connected to geodesics; Euler's cos^2 formula and Meusnier's theorem are omitted.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A natural bridge to GA's geodesic equation (ch8-9) is lost.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Name geodesic curvature and note geodesics are curves with kappa_g = 0, i.e. their acceleration is purely normal to the surface.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Terminology: calling the trace k1 + k2 'the extrinsic curvature' conflicts with standard usage (twice mean curvature; in GR 'extrinsic curvature' is the tensor K_ij with trace K). The symbol K is used for three things.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confusion when moving to ADM or other GR texts.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Introduce mean curvature H = (k1 + k2)/2 and keep 'extrinsic curvature' for the tensor.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Riemann's counting of n(n-1)/2 functions and the claim that curvature on that many planes fixes the metric are presented without caveat, and the lecture is dated 1853 (delivered 1854).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may conclude the Riemann tensor has n(n-1)/2 independent components rather than n^2(n^2-1)/12.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present counting as a heuristic about functions; tabulate component counts 1, 6, 20 for n = 2, 3, 4.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Exercise 30.3 misspells Bertrand; eqn 30.32 writes partial symbols for differentials; F_1 and F_2 use dX^mu for coordinate differentials.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Index hygiene slips in section 30.5: the opening sentence writes K_mu nu with de_mu/dx^mu (a repeated index where e_nu is meant), and eqn 30.48 differentiates with respect to t^mu while mu is also a summed dummy index inside the bracket.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers who are still learning the summation convention may think a repeated index can also be free, and then find the Lagrange-multiplier step (30.48 to 30.49) puzzling, including where the factor of 2 goes.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Rename the free index, e.g. differentiate with respect to t^sigma, and show that d(K_mu nu t^mu t^nu)/dt^sigma = 2 K_sigma nu t^nu, using the symmetry of K. The common factor 2 then cancels against the constraint term.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The book calls K_mu nu 'symmetric' without saying why, and in 30.3 it twice says 'curvature of a plane' when it means a two-dimensional surface.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Symmetry is what makes the principal directions perpendicular (Euler) and the eigenvalues real, so leaving it unexplained hides why the construction works; the 'plane' wording can make learners think a flat plane is being discussed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Point out that de_nu/dx^mu is the mixed second derivative of X, which is symmetric in mu and nu, so its normal part is too. Say 'surface' throughout.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'Which is more curved, a small circle or a large one? How would an ant living on a ball know it is not on a table?' The first targets kappa = 1/rho; the second sets up intrinsic curvature.

Order for novices: turning rate of tangents, osculating circle, parabola picture; then surfaces as quadratic bowls or saddles with two principal curvatures; then the cylinder paradox; then Gauss's insider idea. Frenet-Serret can be skipped by learners heading straight to GR.
For stronger learners emphasize eqn 30.36: the tangential part is the connection, the normal part is K_mu nu. This is the bridge to covariant derivatives and to hypersurface GR.
Check for understanding: ask for k1, k2, K and k1 + k2 of a cylinder of radius 2 (expect -1/2 or +1/2 depending on normal, 0, 0, magnitude 1/2), and why K vanishes.
Check: 'A saddle has principal curvatures +1 and -1. Is it intrinsically curved? What sign?' (Yes, K = -1.)
Ask: 'Why does the metric appear when extremizing normal curvature?' Target answer: unit length of the tangent is measured by g, so the eigenproblem is for g^{-1}K.
Common learner question: 'If the cylinder is flat, why does it look curved?' Answer with angle sums of triangles and unrolling; extrinsic curvature is about the embedding.

Common learner question: 'Does spacetime need a higher-dimensional space to curve into?' No; the whole point of Gauss and Riemann is that curvature is defined internally. Embeddings are visual aids only.
Warn about printed errors before learners attempt checks: sphere height and expansion (p.313), eqn 30.25 minus sign, eqn 30.64 factors of a, eqns 30.68-30.69.
When relating to GA ch11, connect K = R_1212/g with the sphere: R_{theta phi theta phi} = a^2 sin^2 theta, g = a^4 sin^2 theta, K = 1/a^2.
Signal the naming clash between curve torsion here and connection torsion later, and between the book's 'extrinsic curvature' (trace) and the tensor K_ij in GR.

If a learner asks why K_mu nu is symmetric or why the principal directions are perpendicular: de_nu/dx^mu is the mixed second derivative of X, symmetric in mu and nu, so its normal projection K_mu nu is symmetric. A matrix that is symmetric with respect to the metric has real eigenvalues and g-orthogonal eigenvectors, which is Euler's perpendicularity.
